This state/province carries the most sustained municipal hostility to a public queer event in the country. City officials and municipal workers attempted to prevent queer-festival organisers from setting up at their central-district venue, and the city's mayor from the governing conservative party publicly attacked the city police chief for the protection the police afforded the event. Police, however, intervened to stop the municipal workers — an institutional response that partly mitigates the threat.

The festival, the country's second-oldest (since June 2009), has run every year for 17 years, described by its organisers as a form of resistance against hate and discriminatory politics, including editions in 2025 and 2026. This persistence signals that municipal obstruction is real but does not prevent the event, and that the recurring annual counter-mobilisation by a religious-conservative umbrella body spanning this state/province and its neighbouring jurisdiction — about 3,500 adherents from some 1,600 congregations along a 450 m stretch, timed against the festival — creates a high-density confrontational environment for a visible trans visitor during festival season. Outside those specific dates, no recurring street-level hostility data are documented.

A domestic daily (2025): this state/province's queer culture festival — begun June 2009, second-oldest in the country — announced that year's event under an anti-erasure slogan on a pedestrianised central shopping street, saying it has taken place every year without fail for 17 years as resistance to hate and discriminatory politics despite interference; organisers cite a national high-court ruling on local anti-discrimination ordinances as affirming sexual minorities as citizens protected by the constitution.

A religious news outlet (September 2025): a religious-conservative umbrella body spanning this state/province and its neighbouring jurisdiction convened its 17th annual national assembly against queerness in response to the local queer culture festival, gathering roughly 3,500 adherents from about 1,600 congregations at a central square and along a 450 m stretch under anti-homosexuality slogans.
